results.summary: This design plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and outputs the sound wave on uio_out[1:0]. The design requires an external piezo speaker connected across those pins and a 100 kHz clock. Silicon tests confirm it works, including with the new audio Pmod and on a Simon board with a pin modification.

This project implements a neural network built from perceptrons on a single tile. It computes an output based on an 8-bit user input and predefined weight parameters. The result is observed on the 8-bit output pins. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and no details on the network architecture or training.

This is an 8-bit stack machine implemented in SystemVerilog. It uses a single data pin for input, output, and bidirectional communication. The design can be tested in hardware or simulation. The documentation is very sparse, offering only a one-line description and no further details on the instruction set or operation.

This is a miniature programmable interrupt timer inspired by the Intel 8253. It asserts an interrupt pin for one clock cycle when a 16-bit counter reaches zero. Configuration is done via input pins and write enable, with status outputs indicating divider, counter, and interrupt states. The design is tested by setting configuration values and observing the interrupt after a set number of clock cycles.

ChipTune is an 8-bit programmable sound generator that replicates the audio processing unit of vintage video games. It receives input via a serial UART interface and outputs PWM audio along with square, triangle, and noise channels. External hardware needed includes a computer COM port and an analog PWM filter with audio driver. The design is notable for its high utilization and heritage from the TT04 shuttle.

This project implements a multiplexed clock that displays hours and minutes on a 4-digit 7-segment display. It uses buttons to increment hours and minutes and includes configuration pins for common anode or cathode displays. The design requires an external 4-digit 7-segment display and pull-up buttons. Silicon tests show partial functionality, with the counter dot increasing every 15 seconds and minutes incrementing.

This design counts lions moving through a tunnel between a cage and an enclosure, using two sensors to track direction. It increments or decrements a counter based on sensor sequences and displays the count on a 7-segment display. The design requires external sensors and a 7-segment display. The documentation explains the state machine logic but does not include silicon test results.

This project demonstrates matrix-vector multiplication, where a vector is multiplied by a matrix that can be set by the user. It includes a counter and 7-segment display for testing purposes. The documentation is inconsistent, describing a counter rather than the multiplication functionality, and lacks details on how to set the matrix or observe results. The design appears to be a demo with limited practical use.

Despite its title, this design implements a counter that increments every second with a 10 MHz clock, displaying the count on a 7-segment display. The inputs can be used to program a compare value to change the counting speed. The documentation describes only the counter functionality and does not mention sparsity-aware matrix-vector multiplication. The design is likely a template or mislabeled project.

This is a matrix-vector multiplication accelerator that takes a 3x3 weight matrix in Compressed Sparse Row format and a 3-bit spike train. It computes the product and outputs the resulting vector on the output lines. The design uses flags to handshake with a CPU for loading and outputting data. The documentation provides a detailed protocol for testing but does not include silicon results.
